script.opening: (Cheerful, chatty, slightly breathless between sentences.) "Afternoon doc. I've come for my X-ray result — it'll be fine, won't it? It's just the tail end of that chest infection I had, I reckon. I'm a bit puffed going up the stairs but that's just age and being out of shape. We've got a cruise booked for next month — so as long as you can give me something to clear it up, I'll be on my way."

facts.text: If asked what he understands: "The other doctor thought it was a slow chest infection. Just to be sure, she said." Had a course of antibiotics before the X-ray, which didn't make much difference.
About two months now. "Only when I'm doing something. Stairs, the garden." Can manage one flight, then stops. Not breathless at rest or lying flat; no waking at night breathless. No ankle swelling.
A dull, dragging ache in the right side of the chest, there most days, a bit worse on a deep breath. Not crushing, not on exertion only.
If asked: "Trousers are a bit looser" — maybe half a stone in three months. "No blood, no fevers." Mild dry cough. No night sweats, no hoarse voice, no bone pain.

If asked about his job: builder and plasterer for 40 years. If asked about asbestos: "Years of it, back in the eighties. Everyone did. No masks, nothing." Cut and sanded asbestos boards and lagging. Took early retirement at 60.
"About ten years' worth. Stopped fifteen years ago." Drinks a few pints at the weekend.
No regular medicines. No heart, kidney or liver problems he knows of. No TB contacts or recent travel. No allergies.
Married to Jean, two grown-up children nearby. The cruise is for their 40th wedding anniversary.

Jolly and hopeful at first. When the doctor gives a warning shot, go quiet: "(Pause.) Go on." On hearing about fluid: "Fluid? So what's causing it?" If asbestos comes up, say quietly: "Every builder knows what asbestos does. I suppose I've been telling myself it's the infection because I didn't want to think about the other thing." If offered antibiotics, accept gladly (the trap). If told about urgent tests, ask "And the cruise?" then accept: "I'd rather know before I go."

ice.ideas: "It's the tail end of the chest infection — and my age."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — as an ex-builder he knows what asbestos can do and has been pushing the thought away. He doesn't want the anniversary cruise spoilt or to frighten Jean.
ice.expectations: "Something to clear it up so I can get on — and the all-clear for the cruise."

"Every builder knows what asbestos does." — the fear, only if his work is explored.

checkpoints.text: BREAKS the unexpected finding clearly and humanely (warning shot, checks prior understanding, names the pleural effusion) rather than minimising it as "a bit of fluid from the infection" or burying it

Recognises an unexplained UNILATERAL pleural effusion as a red flag requiring urgent investigation for malignancy — not attributing it to the presumed chest infection — and screens weight loss, haemoptysis, appetite and systemic features
Takes and DOCUMENTS the occupational/ASBESTOS history (and smoking), recognising it as the key cue for mesothelioma and asbestos-related disease that raises urgency

Applies NICE NG12: a suspected cancer pathway referral for chest X-ray findings suggesting lung cancer or mesothelioma, judging the unexplained unilateral effusion with weight loss and asbestos exposure as such a finding — to respiratory for thoracic ultrasound, pleural aspiration and CT (BTS 2023)
Holds the differential (malignancy — lung/mesothelioma/metastatic; parapneumonic effusion/empyema; TB; and systemic causes for the record) and does NOT default to antibiotics or "see how it settles"
Responds to his hope and likely fear with warmth — acknowledges the cruise and the wish for it to be nothing, surfaces any worry, and does NOT collude with "it’s just the infection"

Balances honesty (this needs urgent hospital tests now) with calm reassurance and pacing — chunking the news, checking understanding, and reframing the cruise around the scan rather than dismissing his plans coldly

Safety-nets and follows up: makes the urgent referral promptly, explains what the respiratory team will do (CT, pleural tap/biopsy) and timing, gives breathless/unwell red flags and when to seek help, confirms understanding, and arranges to review — ownership of the result, not a wave-off

worked.txt: "Before we talk about the cruise, I need to be straight with you about the X-ray, because it didn’t show quite what we both hoped. Is it okay if we go through it together now?"

"The X-ray shows a collection of fluid around your right lung — we call it a pleural effusion. It’s not just the tail end of an infection clearing; fluid only on one side like this is something we always need to look into properly to find the cause."

"Can I ask about your working life — you were a builder and plasterer? How much did you come across asbestos over the years? … Thank you, that’s genuinely important, and it’s one of the reasons I want this looked at quickly rather than waiting."

"I want to be honest with you. Fluid on one side, with you having lost a bit of weight and that asbestos history, is something we have to investigate urgently — to rule out a problem in the lung or its lining. I’m not telling you that’s what it is, but it would be wrong of me to treat this as just an infection."

"So I’m referring you urgently to the chest specialists — you’ll be seen within two weeks. They’ll do a detailed scan and likely take a sample of the fluid to find the answer. I know the timing’s rotten with the cruise; my honest advice is we get this scan done first — your health has to come before the holiday, and I’ll help you think about the booking."

"This is a lot to take in, and it’s okay to feel thrown. If you become a lot more breathless, cough up blood, or feel really unwell before the appointment, contact us or go to A&E. I’ll get the referral done today and we’ll go through whatever they find, together."

f.learning: An incidental or unexpected abnormal result is OWNED and conveyed honestly: a chest X-ray requested for a presumed infection that returns a UNILATERAL pleural effusion is broken with a warning shot, not minimised as "a bit of fluid". A unilateral effusion is a red flag — bilateral effusions suggest systemic causes (heart failure, hypoalbuminaemia), but a unilateral one, especially with weight loss, demands urgent investigation for malignancy (lung cancer, mesothelioma, metastatic/pleural disease) alongside the differential of parapneumonic effusion/empyema and TB. The occupational/ASBESTOS history is the decisive cue here: years of building/plastering exposure points to mesothelioma and asbestos-related pleural disease and must be elicited and documented (it matters clinically and later for industrial-injury benefits). NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026): refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for chest X-ray findings that suggest lung cancer or mesothelioma (an unexplained unilateral effusion with weight loss and asbestos exposure is reasonably judged such a finding; the effusion itself is not a named criterion); and offer an urgent chest X-ray at 40 and over for one or more unexplained chest or systemic symptoms in anyone exposed to asbestos — to respiratory for thoracic ultrasound, pleural aspiration and CT (BTS Guideline for pleural disease, 2023). The hidden agenda is hopeful minimisation ("just the infection / I’ve a cruise booked / give me something to clear it"), often with quiet fear underneath; the skill is to break the news, hold the hope and fear with warmth, refuse to collude or default to antibiotics, reframe the cruise around the scan, and safety-net and follow up.

knowledge.guideline: BTS Guideline for pleural disease (2023) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · GMC Good medical practice (2024) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard
knowledge.summary: A unilateral pleural effusion with weight loss in an asbestos-exposed ex-smoker is malignancy until proven otherwise. Tell him honestly and refer urgently to respiratory.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for lung cancer if chest X-ray findings suggest lung cancer, or at 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis. Whether an unexplained unilateral effusion counts as a finding suggesting cancer is a clinical judgement; at 64 with weight loss and asbestos exposure it is reasonable to treat it as one, and to discuss with respiratory the same day if unsure.

NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for mesothelioma if chest X-ray findings suggest mesothelioma. It also advises offering an urgent direct-access chest X-ray to assess for mesothelioma in people aged 40 and over with 2 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss), or with 1 or more of them if they have ever smoked or have been exposed to asbestos — he met that when first seen.

Bilateral effusions usually reflect systemic causes such as heart failure or low albumin. A unilateral effusion needs a cause found: malignancy (lung, mesothelioma, metastatic), parapneumonic effusion or empyema, TB and pulmonary embolism are the main considerations.

BTS Guideline for pleural disease (2023): thoracic ultrasound, diagnostic pleural aspiration and CT are the usual first steps for an undiagnosed unilateral effusion, with pleural biopsy if needed. Prepare him for this.

Ask when, where, in what job and for how long, and record it. It raises suspicion of mesothelioma and other asbestos-related disease, and supports any later claim for industrial injuries benefit or compensation.
Breathlessness at rest, rapidly worsening breathlessness, chest pain with collapse, fever with rigors (possible empyema) or haemoptysis need same-day assessment rather than waiting for clinic.

Unexplained unilateral effusion in an asbestos-exposed ex-smoker with weight loss — suspected malignancy, NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

ro.d: Picked up the pause at “asbestos” and the hopeful minimisation, and explored both.
Idea (tail end of an infection), concern (asbestos, cancer), expectation (antibiotics and the cruise).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Brian, I’m Dr Hughes. You’ve come for your X-ray result. Before I go through it, how have you been since you saw my colleague?
model.why: Opens with his perspective and current state

model.text: It’ll be fine, won’t it? Just the tail end of that chest infection. I’m a bit puffed on the stairs, but that’s age. We’ve a cruise booked next month — if you can give me something to clear it up, I’ll be on my way.
I can hear you’re really looking forward to that cruise. Can I check what you were told about why the X-ray was done?
model.why: Checks prior understanding before breaking news

model.text: The other doctor thought it was a slow chest infection. Just to be sure, she said.
Thank you. I need to be straight with you: the X-ray didn’t show quite what we hoped. Is it all right if I go through it now?
(Pause.) Go on.

It shows a collection of fluid around your right lung. We call it a pleural effusion. There’s no sign of an infection in the lung itself. Fluid on one side like this isn’t something an infection usually leaves behind, so we need to find out why it’s there.
model.why: Names the finding plainly; separates it from infection

model.text: Fluid? So what’s causing it?
That’s what we need to find out. Can I ask a few more questions first — they’ll help me get you to the right place quickly.
model.why: Chunks information; moves to targeted history

model.text: How is your breathing now — are you breathless sitting still, or only when you’re moving about?
model.why: Severity and need for same-day care

model.text: Only when I’m doing something. Stairs, the garden.
Have you lost weight, gone off your food, had sweats or fevers, or coughed up any blood?
model.why: Weight loss, systemic and infective features, haemoptysis

model.text: Trousers are a bit looser. No blood, no fevers.
You were a builder and plasterer. Did you ever work with asbestos — sheeting, lagging, cutting boards?
Years of it, back in the eighties. Everyone did. No masks, nothing.
Thank you — that’s important, and I’m writing it in your notes in detail, because it matters for your care and possibly for other reasons later. And you smoked for a while, I see?
About ten years’ worth. Stopped fifteen years ago.
When I mentioned asbestos, you went quiet for a second. What’s going through your mind?
model.why: Picks up the non-verbal cue and surfaces the fear

model.text: Every builder knows what asbestos does. I suppose I’ve been telling myself it’s the infection because I didn’t want to think about the other thing.

That’s a very human thing to do. I want to be honest with you. Fluid on one side, with some weight loss and that asbestos history, means we have to check urgently for a problem in the lung or its lining, including cancer. I’m not saying that’s what it is — there are other causes — but it would be wrong to treat it as an infection.
model.why: Honest about malignancy without asserting a diagnosis

model.text: Right. (Pause.) So no antibiotics then.
No — antibiotics wouldn’t help this, and they’d only delay finding the answer.

Here’s the plan. I’m referring you urgently to the chest specialists today, to be seen within two weeks. They’ll usually do an ultrasound of the chest, take a sample of the fluid with a needle, and arrange a detailed CT scan. Draining some fluid often eases the breathing too.
model.why: NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral; explains the next steps

model.text: And the cruise?

I know this is rotten timing. My honest advice is to get the tests done first — the specialists should be able to give you a much clearer picture within a few weeks. Let’s not cancel anything today; tell your travel insurer about the tests, and decide once you know more.
model.why: Reframes the cruise around the tests without dismissing it

model.text: Fair enough. I’d rather know before I go.
Is there someone you’d like with you at the hospital appointments?
I’ll have company. I’ll tell them tonight.

If you become breathless at rest, much more breathless quickly, cough up blood, get a high temperature with shivers, or have chest pain that won’t settle, don’t wait for the appointment — ring us the same day, or 999 if it’s severe.
It’s a lot to take in. What will you tell them tonight about what I’ve said?
There’s fluid on my lung, it’s not the infection, and I’m seeing the chest doctors within two weeks for a scan and a needle test — maybe because of the asbestos. And the cruise waits till we know.
That’s right. If you’ve not heard within a week, ring us. I’ll book a call with you after the clinic so we can go through what they find together.
model.why: Fail-safe and ownership of the result

social.t: A booked cruise is a real loss. Advise him to tell his travel insurer about pending investigations; decisions about travel are best made once results are known.
Bad news and invasive tests are easier with someone present. Offer written information and encourage him to bring a companion.

legal.t: If mesothelioma or another asbestos-related disease is diagnosed, he may be entitled to Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit and other government compensation schemes, and to a civil claim. A detailed, dated occupational history in the notes supports this.

professional.t: An abnormal CXR requested for suspected infection must be acted on promptly by whoever receives it, not left for the patient to book. GMC Good medical practice (2024): follow up results and act on them.
Share the finding and its significance honestly, at a pace the patient can manage; do not collude with “it’s just the infection”.

community.t: Asthma + Lung UK helpline; Mesothelioma UK and local asbestos support groups if mesothelioma is diagnosed; Macmillan Cancer Support.

redFlags: Unilateral pleural effusion — investigate, not treat as infection
Weight loss, haemoptysis, persistent chest pain
Breathlessness at rest or rapidly worsening; fever with rigors (empyema)
psychosocial: Retired builder and plasterer — asbestos exposure in the 1970s and 1980s
ice: Idea: “Just the tail end of that chest infection”
Concern: what asbestos might mean — unspoken at first
Expectation: a clear X-ray, antibiotics and the cruise

playbook.diagnosis: Moderate right unilateral pleural effusion without consolidation in a 64-year-old asbestos-exposed ex-smoker with 6 weeks of breathlessness, chest discomfort and weight loss. Malignancy (lung cancer or mesothelioma) must be excluded urgently: suspected cancer pathway referral to respiratory under NICE NG12.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “There’s fluid around your right lung. Infections don’t usually leave fluid on one side like this, so we need to find the cause. With your weight loss and asbestos work, that includes checking the lung and its lining for cancer — quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hoping it was the infection, partly because you didn’t want to think about asbestos. That’s understandable — and it’s why I want you seen quickly, so you’re not left wondering.”
management.psychosocial: Defer the cruise decision until results; advise telling the travel insurer; encourage a companion at appointments; record the asbestos history.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to respiratory today
Explain thoracic ultrasound, pleural aspiration and CT
safetyNet: Breathless at rest, rapid worsening, haemoptysis, fever with rigors — same day; 999 if severe
Ring if no appointment within a week
GP call after the clinic visit

pitfalls.intro: This is a results station that becomes a breaking-bad-news station. Candidates fail by minimising the finding, by missing the occupational history, or by delivering the word cancer without care.

items.fail: Calling it fluid from the infection and prescribing antibiotics.
items.why: A unilateral effusion without consolidation needs a cause found; NICE NG12 supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for chest X-ray findings that suggest lung cancer or mesothelioma (the effusion itself is not a named criterion).
items.fix: Name it, explain why it isn’t the infection, refer urgently.

items.why: The occupational history is the key cue for mesothelioma and must be documented.
items.fix: Ask directly about sheeting, lagging, boards; record dates and duration.

items.fail: Missing features that need same-day care.
items.why: Breathlessness at rest or fever with rigors changes the timescale.
items.fix: Ask about breathlessness at rest, fever and haemoptysis before planning.

items.fail: Giving the result before checking what he understands or expects.
items.why: Breaking news without a warning shot or check of understanding is a common Relating fail.
items.fix: “What were you told about why the X-ray was done?” then a warning shot.

items.why: His plans matter to him; brushing past them loses rapport.
items.fix: Acknowledge the timing, advise tests first, defer the decision, mention insurance.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will be in touch”.
items.why: No safety-net, no fail-safe and no ownership of the result.
items.fix: Named red flags, chase if no date, and a booked GP call after the clinic.

wordPics.fail: Calls it “a bit of fluid from the infection” and prescribes antibiotics; or delivers “this could be mesothelioma” bluntly with no plan; never asks about asbestos.
wordPics.pass: Breaks the news with a warning shot, recognises a unilateral effusion as needing urgent investigation, takes the asbestos history and refers urgently with a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: checks prior understanding first; responds to the pause at “asbestos”; is honest about cancer without asserting it; explains what respiratory will do; handles the cruise with empathy; documents exposure for later; teach-back and owned follow-up.

avoid.dont: “It’s just a bit of fluid left over from the infection — let’s try another course of antibiotics.”
avoid.instead: “Fluid on one side isn’t something an infection usually leaves behind, so we need to find out why it’s there.”
avoid.why: Minimising a unilateral effusion and treating empirically delays diagnosis.

avoid.dont: “You’ve got fluid on the lung and with your asbestos it’s probably mesothelioma.”
avoid.instead: “We have to check urgently for a problem in the lung or its lining, including cancer. I’m not saying that’s what it is.”
avoid.why: Honest without delivering an unproven diagnosis.

avoid.instead: “My honest advice is tests first — let’s decide about the cruise once we know more.”
avoid.why: Dismissing his plans coldly loses rapport; reframing keeps him engaged.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for lung cancer if chest X-ray findings suggest lung cancer, or at 40 and over with unexplained haemoptysis. Whether an unexplained unilateral effusion counts as a finding suggesting cancer is a clinical judgement; at 64 with weight loss and asbestos exposure it is reasonable to treat it as one, and to discuss with respiratory the same day if unsure.

NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for mesothelioma if chest X-ray findings suggest mesothelioma. It also advises offering an urgent direct-access chest X-ray to assess for mesothelioma in people aged 40 and over with 2 or more unexplained symptoms (cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss), or with 1 or more of them if they have ever smoked or have been exposed to asbestos — he met that when first seen.

Bilateral effusions usually reflect systemic causes such as heart failure or low albumin. A unilateral effusion needs a cause found: malignancy (lung, mesothelioma, metastatic), parapneumonic effusion or empyema, TB and pulmonary embolism are the main considerations.

BTS Guideline for pleural disease (2023): thoracic ultrasound, diagnostic pleural aspiration and CT are the usual first steps for an undiagnosed unilateral effusion, with pleural biopsy if needed. Prepare him for this.

Ask when, where, in what job and for how long, and record it. It raises suspicion of mesothelioma and other asbestos-related disease, and supports any later claim for industrial injuries benefit or compensation.
Breathlessness at rest, rapidly worsening breathlessness, chest pain with collapse, fever with rigors (possible empyema) or haemoptysis need same-day assessment rather than waiting for clinic.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Asked how he was and what he understood before giving the result.
The cruise, his working life, who will support him through tests.
Picked up the pause at “asbestos” and the hopeful minimisation, and explored both.
Idea (tail end of an infection), concern (asbestos, cancer), expectation (antibiotics and the cruise).
Urgent respiratory referral for thoracic ultrasound, pleural aspiration and CT; in-person review if breathlessness worsens.
Lung cancer, mesothelioma, metastatic disease, parapneumonic effusion or empyema, TB, PE; bilateral systemic causes less likely.
Assessed breathlessness at rest, weight loss, fever and haemoptysis; defined same-day triggers.
Unexplained unilateral effusion in an asbestos-exposed ex-smoker with weight loss — suspected malignancy, NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway.
Urgent referral today, no antibiotics, cruise decision deferred until results, support arranged.
Asbestos exposure documented in detail for clinical and later benefit purposes.
Named red flags and 999 route, chase if no date in a week, GP call after clinic.

social.t: A booked cruise is a real loss. Advise him to tell his travel insurer about pending investigations; decisions about travel are best made once results are known.
Bad news and invasive tests are easier with someone present. Offer written information and encourage him to bring a companion.

legal.t: If mesothelioma or another asbestos-related disease is diagnosed, he may be entitled to Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit and other government compensation schemes, and to a civil claim. A detailed, dated occupational history in the notes supports this.

professional.t: An abnormal CXR requested for suspected infection must be acted on promptly by whoever receives it, not left for the patient to book. GMC Good medical practice (2024): follow up results and act on them.
Share the finding and its significance honestly, at a pace the patient can manage; do not collude with “it’s just the infection”.

community.t: Asthma + Lung UK helpline; Mesothelioma UK and local asbestos support groups if mesothelioma is diagnosed; Macmillan Cancer Support.

redFlags: Unilateral pleural effusion — investigate, not treat as infection
Weight loss, haemoptysis, persistent chest pain
Breathlessness at rest or rapidly worsening; fever with rigors (empyema)
psychosocial: Retired builder and plasterer — asbestos exposure in the 1970s and 1980s
ice: Idea: “Just the tail end of that chest infection”
Concern: what asbestos might mean — unspoken at first
Expectation: a clear X-ray, antibiotics and the cruise

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Moderate right unilateral pleural effusion without consolidation in a 64-year-old asbestos-exposed ex-smoker with 6 weeks of breathlessness, chest discomfort and weight loss. Malignancy (lung cancer or mesothelioma) must be excluded urgently: suspected cancer pathway referral to respiratory under NICE NG12.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “There’s fluid around your right lung. Infections don’t usually leave fluid on one side like this, so we need to find the cause. With your weight loss and asbestos work, that includes checking the lung and its lining for cancer — quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hoping it was the infection, partly because you didn’t want to think about asbestos. That’s understandable — and it’s why I want you seen quickly, so you’re not left wondering.”
management.psychosocial: Defer the cruise decision until results; advise telling the travel insurer; encourage a companion at appointments; record the asbestos history.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a results station that becomes a breaking-bad-news station. Candidates fail by minimising the finding, by missing the occupational history, or by delivering the word cancer without care.

items.fail: Calling it fluid from the infection and prescribing antibiotics.
items.why: A unilateral effusion without consolidation needs a cause found; NICE NG12 supports a suspected cancer pathway referral for chest X-ray findings that suggest lung cancer or mesothelioma (the effusion itself is not a named criterion).
items.fix: Name it, explain why it isn’t the infection, refer urgently.

items.why: The occupational history is the key cue for mesothelioma and must be documented.
items.fix: Ask directly about sheeting, lagging, boards; record dates and duration.

items.fail: Missing features that need same-day care.
items.why: Breathlessness at rest or fever with rigors changes the timescale.
items.fix: Ask about breathlessness at rest, fever and haemoptysis before planning.

items.fail: Giving the result before checking what he understands or expects.
items.why: Breaking news without a warning shot or check of understanding is a common Relating fail.
items.fix: “What were you told about why the X-ray was done?” then a warning shot.

items.why: His plans matter to him; brushing past them loses rapport.
items.fix: Acknowledge the timing, advise tests first, defer the decision, mention insurance.

items.fail: Ending with “the hospital will be in touch”.
items.why: No safety-net, no fail-safe and no ownership of the result.
items.fix: Named red flags, chase if no date, and a booked GP call after the clinic.
